gXEUsl-H6gA.speaker: adnan
gXEUsl-H6gA.speaker_note: his Essentials and Pet Peeves khutbah series; draws on his recent visit to Syria
gXEUsl-H6gA.title: Essentials and Pet Peeves: Internal Cleanliness
gXEUsl-H6gA.one_line: The Prophet gave a poor desert people the habits of wealthy, civilized societies, and then went further by asking them to clean the inside too.
gXEUsl-H6gA.summary: He takes as his starting point Norbert Elias's The Civilizing Process: as societies grow wealthier and more peaceful they develop manners, hygiene, orderly queues, law and restraint from violence. He warns against judging the early Muslims through the lens of our own time, then shows that the Prophet brought exactly these habits to a poor, tribal, unschooled people with no government. He taught them to dress cleanly, make wudu, use the miswak, trim nails and remove hair, stand in straight rows and enter the masjid in order, lower the gaze and respect women, settle disputes by law rather than force, clear the road, eat with manners and reject racism. Drawing on his recent visit to Syria, he contrasts this with Muslim societies today where none of it is practised, though everyone knows the teachings. Revelation, he argues, saves humanity centuries of trial and error by giving the end result at the start; the rujz of Al-Muddaththir is anything that agitates and spoils life. The greater leap was internal: the Prophet asked shepherds to examine their intentions and rid themselves of vanity, arrogance and envy, something not even polished elites do. We have kept the appearance and lost the essence, and each of us should ask what the Quran has actually changed in us.

outline.heading: An essential worth contemplating
outline.gist: He admits he has no neat action plan for this topic but thinks it deserves reflection.

outline.heading: Rujz: shun whatever agitates

outline.heading: Habits kept under the umbrella of religion

outline.heading: The inside matters too
outline.gist: He told people struggling to survive that their feelings and intentions count, and to remove vanity, arrogance and envy.

outline.heading: What even the elite do not do
outline.gist: Polished societies care about dress and order but not about purifying the heart.

outline.heading: Asking a shepherd about his intentions
outline.gist: How he got Bedouins to examine their inner states is almost unimaginable.

outline.heading: Inner purity as part of being civilized
outline.gist: Caring how you feel towards others and checking your intention before acting.

outline.heading: Revelation gives you the end result
outline.gist: Wahy spares humanity social experiments that waste lives; here is how to live well.

outline.heading: Giants we would not recognise
outline.gist: We judge by fabric and appearance and would miss the companions if they walked in today.

outline.heading: Bring the essence back

outline.heading: Has the Quran changed you?

outline.heading: What is still missing
outline.gist: The companions took each teaching and moved forward; we stalled on a plateau.

QTLsVVhhHZc.speaker_note: his Essentials and Pet Peeves khutbah series; follows on from the previous week's khutbah and the week's khaterahs
QTLsVVhhHZc.title: Essentials and Pet Peeves: Defeatist Mentality
QTLsVVhhHZc.one_line: A Muslim must never feel defeated or lesser because the ummah is weak; truth is not measured by wealth, numbers or power.
QTLsVVhhHZc.summary: He explains that last week's khutbah on the civilizing work of the Prophet was meant to protect Muslim youth from a defeatist mentality. Ibn Khaldun observed that the defeated always admire and imitate the victor in dress, speech, slogans and customs, and the ummah today is not the victorious one. The Quran repeatedly warns against being dazzled by others' wealth, numbers, appearance and freedom of movement in the land. After Uhud Allah told the believers not to weaken or grieve, and to ask what they had done wrong; the companions reviewed the battle, owned the archers' mistake, repented and moved on without becoming a symbol of defeat. The Prophet rebuked the companions for admiring a fine gifted garment, saying Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's handkerchiefs in paradise are better, and rebuked 'Umar for weeping over the palm-fibre mat while Persia and Rome enjoyed luxury. He stresses that this is not a call to abandon wealth or ignore what others do well: the Prophet adopted foreign ideas such as the trench and the seal, and Muslims must diagnose their real problems rather than mock the West. The truth is known by itself, not by the men or numbers behind it, so neither the majority nor a rebellious minority is a measure; Islam adheres to the jama'ah. The hadith of the Prophet as judge shows that not even his ruling makes something yours if you know it is not. Judge Islam by its ideals and the Prophet's era, not by Muslims today.

outline.heading: Why he gave last week's khutbah
outline.gist: Today builds on last week; it took him days to see why he shared it.

outline.gist: The real aim was to guard against a defeated mentality in Muslim youth.

outline.heading: Judge Islam by its ideals
outline.gist: Not by how Muslims or Muslim-majority countries behave, but by the Prophet's era.

outline.heading: Truth by numbers is a stock market
outline.gist: Allegiance based on numbers keeps shifting with no consistency.

outline.heading: Neither defeat nor arrogance
outline.gist: Laughing at others for lacking a bidet is not sane either; just stick to what is right.

outline.heading: A vaccine for our youth
outline.gist: Following the truth lets children learn from others without being in awe of them.

outline.heading: Not even the Prophet's ruling
outline.gist: He judged by what he heard; if you know it is your brother's right, do not take it.

outline.heading: Learn from others, hold to the truth
outline.gist: Islam's ideals are mesmerising; benefit from others' experience but adhere only to the truth.

cmDOMhSDviQ.speaker: adnan
cmDOMhSDviQ.speaker_note: Essentials and Pet Peeves khutbah, given while the community is praying away from its usual building; second khutbah in Arabic
cmDOMhSDviQ.title: Essentials and Pet Peeves: Allah Has a Plan for Me
cmDOMhSDviQ.one_line: Five corrections to how Muslims use phrases like 'Allah has a plan for me' and 'Allah only chooses the best for me'.
cmDOMhSDviQ.summary: He apologises for an uncomfortable topic: phrases Muslims say in English and Arabic, such as 'Allah has a plan for me', 'Allah only chose the best for me' and 'there will be ease after this', which are true in themselves but are often said with the wrong meaning. He sets out five points. First, 'God has a plan for me' comes from Jeremiah 29:11 and has no Islamic equivalent; when he asks people what they mean, the answer reveals that they, not Allah, are deciding what counts as good, while Allah has stated the purpose: worship and being tested in who is best in deed. Second, many accept trials only on condition that their life ends in worldly triumph; nobody promised that, most people are already living their high point without noticing, as he admits he once did, and many companions such as Mus'ab and Ja'far gave everything and died poor. Third, these phrases are used to dodge accountability, blaming Allah for the results of one's own choices. Fourth, Islam does not promise that things work out as you want in this life; it promises tests, harshest for the prophets and then the best of people. In the Arabic second khutbah he restates this: Allah alone knows and decides what is good, ease is promised for the hereafter rather than this world, and a life of ease here is worthless if the meeting with Allah is hard. Finally, someone sick for thirty years who dies has his ease in the grave and beyond; without reassessment and accountability these phrases weaken one's deen.

outline.heading: An uncomfortable topic
outline.gist: He apologises in advance and explains why he raises it here.

outline.heading: Phrases Muslims say
outline.gist: 'Allah has a plan for me', 'Allah only chose the best', 'He is the best Protector' in English and Arabic.

outline.heading: Right words, wrong meaning
outline.gist: Said with the wrong understanding these terms are disastrous; he will make five points.

outline.heading: First: 'God has a plan for me' is not ours
outline.gist: The phrase comes from Jeremiah 29:11; he always asks people what they mean by it.

outline.heading: Who decides what is good?
outline.gist: If you judge the plan by your own outcome, you have made yourself the planner.

outline.heading: Allah stated the purpose
outline.gist: We were created to worship and to be tested in who is best in deed, with belief in qadar, good and bad.

outline.heading: Second: trials on condition of a triumphant ending
outline.gist: Many accept hardship only if they end up with wealth, status or success.

outline.heading: Who promised you that?
outline.gist: A man said he was waiting for his up-slope; how does he know he is not in it now?

outline.heading: He missed his own high point
outline.gist: Most people are living their best moment without gratitude; he admits he did too.

outline.heading: You cannot hold Allah to your expectations
outline.gist: There is usually no final triumph; the triumph is how you respond to what you are given.

outline.heading: Mus'ab and Ja'far
outline.gist: Companions gave everything, stayed poor, and Ja'far died soon after returning; put a full stop after 'I accept the trials'.

outline.heading: Third: the phrases erase accountability
outline.gist: After a terrible choice people say 'that is what Allah chose for me'.

outline.heading: What about what you did?
outline.gist: The whole story of existence rests on taking responsibility for our choices.

outline.heading: Not the centre of the universe
outline.gist: Expecting Allah to bail us out of every bad choice borders on blaming Him.

outline.heading: Fourth: Islam promises tests, not ease here
outline.gist: A person is tested by his religion; the prophets most of all; we ask to be servants of kindness, not of testing.

outline.heading: Second khutbah: words that need correcting
outline.gist: In Arabic: Allah wants only good for His servants, but what do we mean by these phrases?

outline.heading: Ease is in the hereafter
outline.gist: What good is an easy life followed by a hard meeting with Allah?

outline.heading: Who knows the good?
outline.gist: Allah chooses ease and hardship for me; I respond with patience and gratitude.

outline.heading: Victory is not written for everyone
outline.gist: Yusuf and the Prophet were given victory; the sick man who dies saw none in this world.

outline.heading: Our gaze moved from the hereafter to this world
outline.gist: That shift is why these phrases became muddled and hard to hear corrected.

outline.heading: Fifth: where is their ease?
outline.gist: Those chronically ill for thirty years who die find their ease in the grave and after.

outline.heading: No reassessment, no accountability
outline.gist: Without self-review a life of difficulty makes no sense and the climb is pointless.

outline.heading: Know what you are saying
outline.gist: Yes, Allah chooses the best and has a plan; understand it for the strength of your deen.

xtJsHg2o9K8.speaker: adnan
xtJsHg2o9K8.speaker_note: his Sunday English tafseer series on the free-will cluster of surahs; recalls saluting the dictator's picture at school in Syria
xtJsHg2o9K8.title: English Tafseer: Surat Al-Mutaffifin 1-17
xtJsHg2o9K8.one_line: Al-Mutaffifin brings consequences into the free-will cluster, opening with the double standard as the root of all ethical corruption.
xtJsHg2o9K8.summary: He recaps the cluster of early Makkan surahs on free will: Al-Takwir made human choice a sacred gift, Al-Infitar showed that it is recorded, and Al-Mutaffifin, one of the last Makkan surahs, adds accountability. No one can coerce your inner allegiance; he recalls having to salute the dictator's picture every morning at school in Syria without believing a word. The surah has four sections: an example of ethical corruption, accountability for corrupt choices, accountability for virtuous ones, and outcomes. Your fiqh choices are the least of your problems; ethical choices are where justice, oppression and life itself are decided, and they decide whom you trust. Those who demand full measure when buying and short others when selling embody the double standard, which reduces morality to one test: ethics applied selectively are mere preferences. The second verse alone would be blameless; the condemnation lies in the double standard, which every listener carries somewhere, from protective brothers who allow themselves what they forbid their sisters, to drivers, to the world's response to Palestinian deaths. He calls it pure evil, since it requires believing you matter more than others. The word appears only here in the Quran. Do they not think they will be resurrected to stand before the Lord of the worlds? After a tajweed aside on the dry Arabic jeem and the heavy letters, he explains sijjin as a prison for those who abused their freedom, the sealed record, the mukadhdhib who goes against his own best judgment and doubles down, the transgressor and the sinner who call revelation ancient fables, and the rust that covers their hearts.

outline.heading: The double standard as pure evil
outline.gist: It requires believing your value is higher than everyone else's.

outline.heading: Not for shoving in other people's faces
outline.gist: Applying these verses only to others is itself a double standard.

outline.heading: The only place this word appears
outline.gist: Mutaffifin is used nowhere else in the Quran; ethical corruption is where questioning will focus.

outline.heading: Rituals matter, but you will be asked about this
outline.gist: Twelve weekly classes run at the centre, yet ethics is where we will be questioned.

outline.heading: Do they not think they will be resurrected?
outline.gist: A tremendous Day when all stand before the Lord of the worlds; no one is special.

outline.heading: From example to accountability
outline.gist: The next two sections mirror each other: accountability for corrupt and virtuous choices.

outline.heading: Tajweed: the dry Arabic jeem
outline.gist: The jeem is not the English j; keep the tongue dry against the palate.

outline.heading: The difficult letters and the hamza
outline.gist: Letters that cannot be prolonged; Arabs added a bounce or eased the hamza, where most differences between readings lie.

outline.heading: Kitab here means fate
outline.gist: The destination already written for the fujjar.

outline.heading: Fujur: an umbrella term for ethical breach
outline.gist: Different from kufr; any choice to act unethically.

outline.heading: Sijjin: a prison for those who abused freedom
outline.gist: Punishments in the Quran mirror the sin; those who misused their will lose it.

outline.heading: A sealed record
outline.gist: Marqum means carved into stone so it cannot fade.

outline.heading: Wayl for the mukadhdhibin
outline.gist: Not simply disbelief, which may be sincere conviction.

outline.heading: Going against your own best judgment
outline.gist: Takdhib is living a lie: you knew the right choice and took the other for gain.

outline.heading: Doubling down
outline.gist: Pride makes people commit to the wrong course; living as if there is no reckoning is a form of denial.

outline.heading: Behaviour exposes belief
outline.gist: Claiming to believe in the Day while never preparing or repaying debts now.

outline.heading: Every transgressor and sinner
outline.gist: Those who harm others and those who harm themselves are the ones who deny the Day.

outline.heading: Fables of the ancients
outline.gist: The virtuous have nothing to fear from accountability; those who want the scales tipped call it myth.

outline.heading: Easier not to believe
outline.gist: Belief means your choices matter and you must think about right and wrong.

outline.heading: Rust on the heart
outline.gist: Accumulated sin covers the heart so it can no longer sense right and wrong; more next week.

quran.point: Woe to the defrauders who take full measure but give less.
Do they not think they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day?

83:14.ar: كَلَّاۖ بَلۡۜ رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم مَّا كَانُواْ يَكۡسِبُونَ
83:14.en: No! Rather, the stain has covered their hearts of that which they were earning

83:15.ar: كَلَّآ إِنَّهُمۡ عَن رَّبِّهِمۡ يَوۡمَئِذࣲ لَّمَحۡجُوبُونَ
83:15.en: No! Indeed, from their Lord, that Day, they will be partitioned

83:16.en: Then indeed, they will [enter and] burn in Hellfire

83:17.ar: ثُمَّ يُقَالُ هَٰذَا ٱلَّذِي كُنتُم بِهِۦ تُكَذِّبُونَ
83:17.en: Then it will be said [to them], "This is what you used to deny

83:18.ar: كَلَّآ إِنَّ كِتَٰبَ ٱلۡأَبۡرَارِ لَفِي عِلِّيِّينَ
83:18.en: No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'illiyyun

83:19.en: And what can make you know what is 'illiyyun

83:20.en: It is [their destination recorded in] a register inscribed

83:21.en: Which is witnessed by those brought near [to Allah]

83:22.en: Indeed, the righteous will be in pleasure

83:24.en: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of pleasure

83:25.en: They will be given to drink [pure] wine [which was] sealed

83:26.ar: خِتَٰمُهُۥ مِسۡكࣱۚ وَفِي ذَٰلِكَ فَلۡيَتَنَافَسِ ٱلۡمُتَنَٰفِسُونَ
83:26.en: The last of it is musk. So for this let the competitors compete

83:27.en: And its mixture is of Tasneem

83:28.en: A spring from which those near [to Allah] drink

83:29.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ أَجۡرَمُواْ كَانُواْ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ يَضۡحَكُونَ
83:29.en: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed

83:30.en: And when they passed by them, they would exchange derisive glances

83:31.ar: وَإِذَا ٱنقَلَبُوٓاْ إِلَىٰٓ أَهۡلِهِمُ ٱنقَلَبُواْ فَكِهِينَ
83:31.en: And when they returned to their people, they would return jesting

83:32.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَوۡهُمۡ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ لَضَآلُّونَ
83:32.en: And when they saw them, they would say, "Indeed, those are truly lost

83:33.en: But they had not been sent as guardians over them

83:34.ar: فَٱلۡيَوۡمَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مِنَ ٱلۡكُفَّارِ يَضۡحَكُونَ
83:34.en: So Today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers

83:36.ar: هَلۡ ثُوِّبَ ٱلۡكُفَّارُ مَا كَانُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
83:36.en: Have the disbelievers [not] been rewarded [this Day] for what they used to do

XZ6PkSokBbs.speaker: adnan
XZ6PkSokBbs.speaker_note: his Sunday English tafseer series on the free-will cluster; Canadian winters and parenting asides
XZ6PkSokBbs.title: English Tafseer: Surat Al-Mutaffifin 14-36
XZ6PkSokBbs.one_line: We seal our own fate: the rust that keeps light from the heart, the mirrored destinations of sijjin and 'illiyyin, and a competition worth living for.
XZ6PkSokBbs.summary: He recaps the cluster: choice is a divine gift, it is recorded, and it has consequences. Sijjin is a prison where those who misused their freedom lose it, and kitab here means a sealed fate, but what determines it is what we ourselves wrote, like results that follow from an exam you sat. After death sincerity and du'a no longer count; the book is closed. Only the transgressor and the sinner reject the Day of Reckoning, since even an atheist father would warn his own children away from alcohol, drugs, gambling and promiscuity; wanting for the world what you refuse for your family is moral corruption. Sin forms rust over the heart, the mixing pot of everything we take in, so the light of Allah cannot reach it and good deeds feel like swimming upstream. Occasionally Allah pierces it, as Ramadan does each year like the first spring sun after a Canadian winter, and the nafs works to keep it sealed. Those who keep the rust are veiled from seeing their Lord. Never live a lie, even a small one: the wife of al-'Aziz harmed Yusuf yet never lied to herself, and that saved her. The third section mirrors the second: the abrar's record is in 'illiyyin, described with the same two words as sijjin. The muqarrabun are drawn close by Allah; closeness is figurative and emotional, which is what most people who come to him struggle with. The faces of the people of paradise show their bliss as they drink sealed nectar ending in musk, mixed from the spring of tasnim. Tanafus comes from breath: live every breath for this goal, competing with yourself, as 'Umar competed with Abu Bakr. The surah ends with the mockers mocked and the question of whether the disbelievers were paid back.

outline.heading: Recap: choice as a recorded gift
outline.gist: The cluster on free will; your choice exists because Allah chose for you to choose.

outline.heading: Consequences and the four sections
outline.gist: Example of corruption, accountability for corrupt and virtuous choices, then outcomes.

outline.heading: Sijjin and a predetermined fate
outline.gist: A prison where misused freedom is lost; the fate is written.

outline.heading: We write our own fate
outline.gist: Like exam results, the outcome follows from what you wrote; logic-free readings try to escape this.

outline.heading: When choice stops mattering
outline.gist: After death all sincerity and du'a mean nothing; the book is closed.

outline.heading: Yawm al-din: the day of repaying debts
outline.gist: Everyone pays what they owe and receives what they are owed.

outline.heading: Only the transgressor and sinner refuse it
outline.gist: Someone living ethically has no reason to deny the Day.

outline.heading: What an atheist father would tell his son
outline.gist: Avoid alcohol, drugs and gambling, even without religion.

outline.heading: What you want for the world but not your daughter
outline.gist: That double standard is moral corruption to the core.

outline.heading: Teenagers and the cloud before their brains
outline.gist: They think rules only ruin their fun.

outline.heading: Parents who cannot say no
outline.gist: Some feel too hypocritical to enforce what they know is right and lie to themselves for decades.

outline.heading: Swimming upstream
outline.gist: When the heart produces no desire for good, every act of worship is a struggle and people give up.

outline.heading: The dark spot and the soil without sun
outline.gist: Sins without repentance blacken the heart; nothing grows without light.

outline.heading: When Allah pierces the rust
outline.gist: A figurative layer; sometimes light breaks through and you find yourself reaching for the Quran.

outline.heading: Ramadan as the first spring sun
outline.gist: Like sun after a Canadian winter; the nafs then works to keep the heart sealed.

outline.heading: Veiled from their Lord
outline.gist: Those who kept the barrier in this life will not see Him on that Day.

outline.heading: This is what you denied
outline.gist: They enter the Fire and are told this is what they called false.

outline.heading: Never live a lie, even a small one
outline.gist: Small lies normalise the feeling and pave the way for bigger ones.

outline.heading: The wife of al-'Aziz never lied to herself
outline.gist: She admitted Yusuf was truthful and that she had not betrayed him in secret.

outline.heading: No longer the villain
outline.gist: Her honesty with herself saved her; if you are wrong, do not spend a moment convincing yourself otherwise.

outline.heading: The abrar and 'illiyyin
outline.gist: Birr is the highest virtue; their record is in the high ranks.

outline.heading: Opposites described identically
outline.gist: Sijjin and 'illiyyin share the same words, a sealed written fate.

outline.heading: Every life is a story we are writing
outline.gist: The fate follows from the book we author.

outline.heading: The muqarrabun and the feeling of distance
outline.gist: Most people's struggle is emotional: they feel far from Allah.

outline.heading: Closeness Allah grants
outline.gist: You cannot decide to be close; you decide your behaviour and He draws you near.

outline.heading: On couches, looking
outline.gist: Beholding what no imagination has conceived.

outline.heading: The radiance of bliss on their faces
outline.gist: The camera turns to their faces since words cannot describe what they see.

outline.heading: Sealed nectar ending in musk
outline.gist: A drink no hand has touched, sealed like an unopened product.

outline.heading: Tanafus: live every breath for this
outline.gist: From nafas, breath: compete towards the goal, not against each other.

outline.heading: Competing with yourself
outline.gist: If there is competition with others, it is one where you want them to succeed too.

outline.heading: 'Umar and Abu Bakr
outline.gist: 'Umar gave half his wealth hoping to outdo Abu Bakr, who gave all of it.

outline.heading: Mixed from tasnim
outline.gist: A spring whose nature we are not told; there must be something in it.

outline.heading: They used to laugh at the believers
outline.gist: The criminals winked at them in mockery as they passed.

outline.heading: Jokes taken home
outline.gist: They called the believers misguided; today the believers laugh as they recline and look.

12:52.ar: ذَٰلِكَ لِيَعۡلَمَ أَنِّي لَمۡ أَخُنۡهُ بِٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي كَيۡدَ ٱلۡخَآئِنِينَ
12:52.en: That is so al-'Azeez will know that I did not betray him in [his] absence and that Allah does not guide the plan of betrayers

12:53.ar: ۞وَمَآ أُبَرِّئُ نَفۡسِيٓۚ إِنَّ ٱلنَّفۡسَ لَأَمَّارَةُۢ بِٱلسُّوٓءِ إِلَّا مَا رَحِمَ رَبِّيٓۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
12:53.en: And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful

12:54.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلۡمَلِكُ ٱئۡتُونِي بِهِۦٓ أَسۡتَخۡلِصۡهُ لِنَفۡسِيۖ فَلَمَّا كَلَّمَهُۥ قَالَ إِنَّكَ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ لَدَيۡنَا مَكِينٌ أَمِينࣱ‏
12:54.en: And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself." And when he spoke to him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted

12:55.ar: قَالَ ٱجۡعَلۡنِي عَلَىٰ خَزَآئِنِ ٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ إِنِّي حَفِيظٌ عَلِيمࣱ‏
12:55.en: [Joseph] said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian

12:56.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَتَبَوَّأُ مِنۡهَا حَيۡثُ يَشَآءُۚ نُصِيبُ بِرَحۡمَتِنَا مَن نَّشَآءُۖ وَلَا نُضِيعُ أَجۡرَ ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:56.en: And thus We established Joseph in the land to settle therein wherever he willed. We touch with Our mercy whom We will, and We do not allow to be lost the reward of those who do good

12:57.ar: وَلَأَجۡرُ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ خَيۡرࣱ لِّلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَكَانُواْ يَتَّقُونَ
12:57.en: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were fearing Allah

GXd6yd9Si14.speaker: adnan
GXd6yd9Si14.speaker_note: his Saturday Arabic tafsir of Surat Yusuf; Arabic throughout
GXd6yd9Si14.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Yusuf 12:52-57
GXd6yd9Si14.one_line: The wife of al-'Aziz never betrayed the truth within herself; the soul that commands evil and how to train it; and Yusuf asking for the storehouses.
GXd6yd9Si14.summary: He returns to the confession of the wife of al-'Aziz, an often overlooked verse. Like the Arabs, the Egyptians believed in Allah but mixed that belief with shirk, which is why she could say that Allah does not guide the plots of betrayers. In every dispute there are two kinds of people: one twists the facts in his mind until he believes he was right, the other knows in private that he wronged someone even if pride stops him admitting it publicly. Not betraying in the unseen is the second. Nobody in the story of Yusuf turns out to be a villain; she repented and, by some reports, Yusuf later married her. People are not born good or evil; each carries potential for both and can repent. He holds that 'I do not absolve myself' is her speech, not Yusuf's as al-Suddi and others said. One unadmitted mistake breeds another, as lies need more lies. The nafs is born when the ruh meets the body; it commands evil only in its results, because it seeks survival and advantage for you alone, like a three-year-old who will not share or a child counting the falafel. You cannot kill it, only train it, and you must keep watching it, checking even your good deeds for its share. Tazkiyah is one of three pillars of the deen and a goal of every messenger, and it is a path walked until death, not a destination. The king then takes Yusuf as his own, makin and amin; Yusuf asks for the storehouses because he was the most competent, which Ibn 'Ashur says obliges a capable person to step forward, unlike 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah. He criticises the unqualified who run mosques, hospitals and charities. The final verses show that every hardship, especially the unjust prison, brought out Yusuf's character, yet the reward of the hereafter is better even had he never left prison.

outline.heading: Recap: the confession of the wife of al-'Aziz
outline.gist: The king questioned the women and she admitted she sought to seduce him.

outline.heading: Belief in Allah mixed with shirk
outline.gist: Like the Arabs, the Egyptians knew Allah; her words show she knew Him.

outline.heading: Two kinds of people in a dispute
outline.gist: One twists the facts until he believes he was right; the other knows inside that he wronged.

outline.heading: Repeat a falsehood until it becomes truth
outline.gist: People and media can convince themselves of lies for decades.

outline.heading: No villain in the story of Yusuf
outline.gist: He hated her as a child until he learned Yusuf married her later.

outline.heading: Betraying in the unseen
outline.gist: In divorces and inheritance disputes each side's story shares nothing with the other's.

outline.heading: No one is born good or evil
outline.gist: People are like mines; anyone can repent, as she did and was forgiven.

outline.heading: Her words, not Yusuf's
outline.gist: He disagrees with al-Suddi and others who attributed 'I do not absolve myself' to Yusuf.

outline.heading: One lie needs another
outline.gist: Because she did not admit the first mistake it grew into accusation and prison.

outline.heading: The soul that commands evil
outline.gist: Every nafs commands evil except at moments Allah has mercy; even prophets train theirs.

outline.heading: The nafs born of ruh and body
outline.gist: Breathed from His spirit; the nafs is the earthly consciousness we share with animals.

outline.heading: The lion that kills the cubs
outline.gist: Nature documentaries hide what the selfish nafs looks like.

outline.heading: The three-year-old who will not share
outline.gist: A child is a nafs without reason: everything for itself.

outline.heading: Counting the falafel
outline.gist: The adult feels it too but is restrained by shame.

outline.heading: Evil in its results, not its essence
outline.gist: It seeks your survival and advantage; you cannot kill it, only train it.

outline.heading: Question its desires
outline.gist: Oppose the nafs and Shaytan; check what share it takes even in good deeds.

outline.heading: Praying at three in the morning
outline.gist: The nafs cannot understand a deed that brings no worldly gain or praise.

outline.heading: Constant watch over the self
outline.gist: Desire can move from haram to halal until it follows what the Prophet brought.

outline.heading: What the nafs can lead to
outline.gist: Pharaoh's claim to divinity, Iblis's refusal, Qarun and Abu Jahl.

outline.heading: Like a spoiled child
outline.gist: Left unweaned it grows on its desires; restraint is the human difference.

outline.heading: Ihsan: the forgotten third pillar
outline.gist: Islam, iman and ihsan; purification is a stated purpose of every messenger.

outline.heading: The scholars' love of worship
outline.gist: 'Uthman completing the Quran in one rak'ah; read Sayd al-Khatir or al-Tibyan.

outline.heading: Make purifying yourself your main work
outline.gist: Free it from vanity, envy and miserliness and replace them with mercy and generosity.

outline.heading: A path, not a destination
outline.gist: Tazkiyah continues until you meet Allah; she is not mentioned again.

outline.heading: Bring him to me
outline.gist: The king wants Yusuf for himself after the confession clears his name.

outline.heading: Makin and amin
outline.gist: A position of authority and the king's full trust.

outline.heading: Put me over the storehouses
outline.gist: Hafiz and 'alim: he can guard the resources and knows the quantities.

outline.heading: Ibn 'Ashur: the capable must step forward
outline.gist: Hiding competence under false humility is not allowed.

outline.heading: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah
outline.gist: He was told not to ask for leadership because others were as qualified; Yusuf was not in that position.

outline.heading: No false humility
outline.gist: Yusuf says 'I know' when he knows and 'I do not' when he does not.

outline.heading: Unqualified people running mosques
outline.gist: They do not know how to run a masjid or what it is for.

outline.heading: Hospitals and charities run by the wrong people
outline.gist: Intelligence in one field does not qualify someone to run another.

outline.heading: Intellectual humility
outline.gist: Turn down roles you are not qualified for, even when called a saviour.

outline.heading: Leading the prayer
outline.gist: Step forward only if no one is more qualified, and do not hold back if you are.

outline.heading: Ten years pass before the next scene
outline.gist: Two verses of divine commentary come first.

outline.heading: Thus We established Yusuf in the land
outline.gist: Every detail of the story was preparing him; he could settle wherever he wished.

outline.heading: Hardship revealed his character

quran.point: I did not betray him in secret; I do not absolve myself, the soul commands evil.
If you ask them who created the heavens and earth they will say Allah.
A messenger who recites His verses and purifies them.
Ibrahim's prayer for a messenger who would teach and purify.
Allah's favour in sending a messenger who purifies them.
The king: bring him to me; Yusuf: put me over the storehouses.

hadith.gist: People are like mines: the best of them in Jahiliyyah are the best in Islam if they understand.
None of you believes until his desire follows what I have brought.

Told not to seek leadership because others were as qualified.

takeaways: In any dispute, admit to yourself when you were wrong, even if you cannot yet say it aloud.
Never write anyone off; every person can repent.
Question what your nafs gains from each deed, even good ones.
Step forward where you are truly the most competent, and step aside where you are not.
Do not demand a worldly reward for your patience.

QrJlzsGkTH4.speaker: adnan
QrJlzsGkTH4.speaker_note: Thursday-night khaterah introducing the next day's khutbah topic; mentions slipping on the ice on his way in
QrJlzsGkTH4.title: The Magnitude of Reward and the Magnitude of Trial
QrJlzsGkTH4.one_line: Allah tests those He loves, and the only choice left to us is whether we meet the test with contentment or with resentment.
QrJlzsGkTH4.summary: On a Thursday night he narrates the hadith he will build on in the next day's khutbah: the greatness of the reward is with the greatness of the trial, and when Allah loves a people He tests them; whoever is content has contentment, and whoever is displeased has displeasure. Reward correlates with the severity and number of trials. The Prophet anticipates the person who says 'if this is love, I do not want it': accepting or objecting changes nothing about what happens. You cannot ask to move to the category of small reward and fewer tests. The only real choice is whether you are grateful and content, or whether you place yourself among the disgruntled. He draws the lesson that obsessing over what we cannot control ruins our mindset and harms us, while what we can control is right in front of us: making better choices.

outline.heading: The night of salawat and tomorrow's topic
outline.gist: He introduces the hadith that will lead into the next day's khutbah.

outline.heading: Reward matches the trial
outline.gist: The size of the reward correlates with the size and number of tests.

outline.heading: When Allah loves a people He tests them
outline.gist: The Prophet answers the person who says 'if this is love, I do not want it'.

outline.heading: Accepting changes nothing about what happens
outline.gist: You cannot ask to be moved out of the category.

outline.heading: The only choice you have
outline.gist: Either gratitude and contentment, or resentment; you do not get a third option.

outline.heading: Focus on what you control
outline.gist: Obsessing over what we cannot control harms us; better choices are in our hands.

themes.note: Trials come with reward and are a sign of Allah's love.

themes.label: Contentment and acceptance (ridha)
themes.note: Contentment is the only real choice in the face of trials.

themes.note: Focus on what you can control.

hadith.gist: The greatness of the reward is with the greatness of the trial; when Allah loves a people He tests them. Whoever is content has contentment, and whoever is displeased has displeasure.

maxims: You do not get to choose a smaller reward
takeaways: See trials as carrying reward and as a sign of Allah's love.
Choose contentment, since resentment changes nothing.
Put your energy into the choices you can control.

qzQ50FiDf3M.speaker: adnan
qzQ50FiDf3M.speaker_note: khaterah series narrating hadiths around his current khutbah themes
qzQ50FiDf3M.title: Clarity of Lifestyle #2: 'Umar and the Palm-Fibre Mat
qzQ50FiDf3M.one_line: 'Umar wept at the Prophet's empty room and was rebuked: wealth was never the measure of success, and the Prophet was the richest person who ever lived.
qzQ50FiDf3M.summary: He narrates 'Umar's entry into the Prophet's room, recorded by al-Bukhari: the Prophet lay on a palm-fibre mat whose marks covered his side, and the room held nothing but a few old hides. 'Umar wept, an unusual sight, and in another narration asked the Prophet to pray that Allah make his ummah wealthy like the kings of Persia and Rome. The Prophet called him 'son of al-Khattab', a pointed reminder of a father who never accepted Islam, and asked whether he was in doubt: those people were given their good things early in this life; are you not content that we have the hereafter? 'Umar asked him to seek forgiveness for him. He explains that for a moment 'Umar compared the ummah to others by the metric of wealth and felt lesser, and the Prophet did not let it pass. This is not a call to avoid building wealth, which the companions did. Rather, money has never been the metric of success, religious or not. True wealth is defined differently: the Prophet was the wealthiest person ever to live, and by comparison anyone with stuffed pillows at home is poor.

outline.heading: The palm-fibre mat and the empty room
outline.gist: 'Umar saw the marks across the Prophet's body and nothing in his house.

outline.heading: 'Umar weeps
outline.gist: A rare sight; he felt sincerely upset in that moment.

outline.heading: Ask Allah to make your ummah wealthy
outline.gist: In another narration 'Umar points to the wealth of Persia and Rome.

outline.heading: Son of al-Khattab
outline.gist: Calling him by his father's name was a pointed reminder.

outline.heading: They were given their good things early
outline.gist: 'Umar accepts and asks the Prophet to seek forgiveness for him.

outline.heading: A moment of comparison by wealth
outline.gist: 'Umar briefly felt self-conscious belonging to a poorer ummah.

outline.heading: The Prophet did not let it pass
outline.gist: This is not a call to stop building wealth, which the companions did.

outline.heading: Money has never been the metric
outline.gist: It can be added to other measures but is never the measure of success.

outline.heading: The wealthiest person who ever lived
outline.gist: True wealth is defined differently; compared with him we are all poor.

maxims: Money has never been the metric of success

stories.point: Wept at the Prophet's poverty and was corrected.

takeaways: Do not judge a person or a community by its wealth.
Build wealth if you wish, but never let it define success.
Remember that true richness is defined differently.

BL55s8lYQGQ.speaker: adnan
BL55s8lYQGQ.speaker_note: khaterah series narrating hadiths around his khutbah themes until the community returns to its building
BL55s8lYQGQ.title: Clarity of Lifestyle #3: Even If I Rule in Your Favour
BL55s8lYQGQ.one_line: The Prophet warned that even his own ruling does not make something yours if you know it belongs to your brother: stand by what is right whatever the numbers.
BL55s8lYQGQ.summary: He explains that until the community returns to its usual building he will narrate hadiths connected to the khutbahs. The week's theme was not being fooled by numbers: do what is right whether many or few do it, and do not feel defeated as a true minority in the world, since identity should be nothing more than commitment to the truth. He narrates from Umm Salamah, in al-Bukhari's wording: I am only human, and some of you may argue better than others; if I rule in someone's favour and give him what belongs to his brother, let him not take it, for I am giving him a piece of fire. No one could have a stronger claim than a ruling from the Prophet himself, yet he says it does not settle the matter. The lesson is to adhere to what is right regardless, using no other metric than the essence of righteousness in what you pursue or take.

outline.heading: Hadiths until we return home
outline.gist: He will narrate hadiths connected to the khutbahs while away from the usual building.

outline.heading: Not fooled by numbers
outline.gist: Do what is right whether many or few do it; do not feel defeated as a minority.

outline.heading: Identity as commitment to the truth
outline.gist: Our identity should simply be commitment to what is right.

outline.heading: I am only human
outline.gist: Some argue better than others; if I give you your brother's right, do not take it.

outline.heading: No stronger claim than his ruling
outline.gist: Imagine having the Prophet himself rule in your favour.

outline.heading: A piece of fire
outline.gist: Even his judgment can be mistaken; what matters is what is right.

outline.heading: Use no other metric
outline.gist: Only the essence of righteousness in what you pursue or take.

maxims: Not even a ruling in your favour makes it yours
takeaways: Do not take what you know is not yours, whatever ruling you obtain.
Judge what you follow by its rightness, not by how many follow it.

BietL4-zUQ0.speaker: adnan
BietL4-zUQ0.speaker_note: khaterah series expanding a hadith he referred to in the khutbah
BietL4-zUQ0.title: Clarity of Lifestyle #4: Glad Tidings to the Strangers
BietL4-zUQ0.one_line: 'Islam began strange' was meant to keep a faithful minority from feeling defeated, not to make rebellion against the majority a virtue.
BietL4-zUQ0.summary: He narrates a hadith he only referred to in the khutbah: Islam began strange and will return strange as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers. Asked who they are, the Prophet said those who reform when people are corrupt. Its other wordings place it at the end of time, describing people who flee with their religion under persecution. Yet a whole current used this hadith to argue that being right requires opposing the norm and the jama'ah, building a rebellion mindset that is against things for the sake of it. This ignores the many hadiths urging unity and togetherness, and appeals to people who want to feel like saviours among the lost, producing a cancerous cell in a body already sick. The real benefit of the hadith is that a minority holding to what is right should not feel defeated. Muslims today are caught between two extremes, those dazzled by the majority who lose their identity and those who must belong to a group rebelling against everyone. The answer is to stand by what we know to be true and to search for it when we do not.

outline.heading: A hadith from the khutbah
outline.gist: Adhering to truth rather than being dazzled by numbers, and the urge to be in a minority.

outline.heading: Islam began strange
outline.gist: A small group that did not fit in, and so it will end.

outline.heading: Those who reform when people are corrupt
outline.gist: Glad tidings to those who keep calling for reform.

outline.heading: The end of time and the rebellion mindset
outline.gist: Other wordings point to the end of time; some made opposing the norm a virtue.

outline.heading: Ignoring a hundred hadiths on unity
outline.gist: Using his words to suit an agenda, especially a political one.

outline.heading: The appeal of being a saviour
outline.gist: A cancerous cell in a body already failing from other diseases.

outline.heading: What the hadith is for
outline.gist: Do not feel defeated as a small minority on what is right; it is not a call to seek minority status.

outline.heading: Between two extremes
outline.gist: Neither dazzled by the majority nor rebelling against everyone; stand by and seek the truth.

themes.label: Extremism, bad religiosity and distorted practice
themes.note: Misusing the hadith of the strangers to justify rebellion.

themes.label: Accepting the truth, open-mindedness and honest feedback
themes.note: Stand by the truth, not by numbers either way.

themes.label: Unity of the ummah
themes.note: Many hadiths prioritise unity and togetherness.

themes.label: Reform (islah)
themes.note: The strangers are those who reform when people are corrupt.

hadith.gist: Islam began strange and will return strange as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers.
Asked who the strangers are, he said: those who set things right when people become corrupt.

maxims: Not dazzled by the majority, not in love with the minority
takeaways: Do not feel defeated when you are among few on what is right.
Do not oppose the norm just to feel righteous.
Seek the truth and hold to it whatever its popularity.

DWH98NQn-jk.speaker: adnan
DWH98NQn-jk.speaker_note: short khaterah, mostly Arabic narration with English commentary
DWH98NQn-jk.title: Clarity of Lifestyle #5: Settle Your Wrongs Today
DWH98NQn-jk.one_line: Whoever has wronged his brother should seek release today, because on the Day of Judgement payment is made in good deeds.
DWH98NQn-jk.summary: He narrates the hadith: whoever has wronged his brother in his honour or anything else should seek to be released from it today, before a day when there is neither dinar nor dirham; if he has good deeds they will be taken in proportion to the wrong, and if not, the sins of the one he wronged will be placed on him. He adds the warning that such a person may then be thrown into the Fire. Making amends in this life may be hard and humiliating, whatever it costs in money, time or honour, and even physical and verbal abuse all at once is cheaper than having to hand over a single good deed. Good deeds are the most expensive currency there is, and we can barely look after our own.

outline.heading: Seek release today
outline.gist: Whoever has wronged his brother should settle it now.

outline.heading: Paid in good deeds
outline.gist: No dinar or dirham, only good deeds taken and sins placed on him.

outline.heading: Any price now is cheaper
outline.gist: Money, time, honour, even abuse, all cost less than one good deed.

outline.heading: The most expensive currency
outline.gist: We can barely carry our own deeds, let alone someone else's sins.

themes.label: The unlawfulness of harm and protecting others
themes.note: Settle wrongs done to others before the Day of Judgement.

themes.label: Tawbah: repentance and returning to Allah
themes.note: Repentance for wrongs against people requires seeking release.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Good deeds as the currency of that Day.

hadith.gist: Whoever has wronged his brother should seek release today before there is no dinar or dirham; his good deeds will be taken, or the other's sins placed on him.

maxims: Good deeds are the most expensive currency
takeaways: Seek forgiveness from anyone you have wronged now, whatever it costs.
Do not underestimate how costly unsettled wrongs will be.
